opus-5.5.text:
For me it comes down to a few questions I ask myself, and I try to be honest with the answers.

The first is whether I'd still want to work on this problem even if the company didn't work out. Startups are long and painful, and there will be many moments when the external rewards just aren't there. If the only thing keeping you going is the hope of a big outcome, I think that's fragile. When I started working on Taichi, it began as something I genuinely cared about as a researcher. I wanted to make high-performance graphics and simulation programming easier. That intrinsic motivation carried me through a lot of uncertainty.

The second question is whether I have some unfair advantage, something about my background, skills, or insight that makes me better positioned than most people to solve this problem. It doesn't have to be dramatic. It could be that you've spent years deep in a niche and you see a pain point others don't. If anyone could do it equally well, you're probably in a crowded race.

Third is timing. Is the world ready for this now? A good idea five years too early can look exactly like a bad idea. So I look at whether the underlying technology and the market are actually converging.

And finally, the people. Who would I be building this with? Co-founders and early team members matter more than almost anything else. If I don't trust them deeply and enjoy working with them, no opportunity is worth it.

I'd also say that it's okay to say no. Opportunities come and go, and the cost of committing several years of your life to the wrong thing is very high. So I try to be patient and wait for something where all of these line up, or at least most of them.

r001.rationale: The response discusses timing and market convergence, but does not say that consensus means it is generally too late unless one has vastly greater resources.

r002.rationale: It does not identify physical capacity as a limit on sustained founder effort.

r003.rationale: It emphasizes intrinsic motivation, but does not state that the opportunity must coincide with a time when the founder is willing to strive.

r004.rationale: It does not mention family caregiving responsibilities or their effect on startup intensity.

r005.rationale: It recommends genuine personal interest, but does not pair that with choosing a large market.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I actually had to answer in a very concrete way, because when I finished my PhD at MIT I had a pretty comfortable set of options. I could have gone to a big lab, or stayed in academia, and instead I ended up starting Taichi Graphics. So let me tell you how I thought about it.

The first thing I look at is whether the problem is one I would work on anyway, even if nobody paid me. Taichi started as a side project. I was writing physics simulations and I was frustrated that writing high-performance GPU code was so painful, so I built a compiler to make it easier. I kept working on it for years before there was any company around it. If you find yourself doing that, it's a strong signal, because a startup is going to be much harder than a side project, and the only thing that carries you through the hard parts is genuinely caring about the problem.

The second thing is whether there are real people asking for it. Not people saying "that sounds cool," but people actually using the thing, filing issues, complaining when it breaks. Open source gave me that feedback loop for free. When I saw researchers, game developers, and people in industry picking up Taichi and building things I never expected, that told me the need was real and not just in my head.

The third thing is timing. Technology has windows. GPU computing, differentiable simulation, the whole wave of people needing to write parallel code who are not systems experts, all of that was converging. If I had waited five more years, somebody else would have done it, and if I had done it five years earlier, the hardware and the community would not have been ready. You can't control timing perfectly, but you can notice when the window is open.

And then honestly, the last part is about yourself. I asked whether I could tolerate being bad at a lot of things for a while. As a researcher you're trained to be an expert. As a founder you are suddenly doing hiring, fundraising, talking to customers, and you're a beginner at all of it. If that idea excites you more than it scares you, that's a good sign. If it mostly scares you, that's fine too, it just means a different path might fit better.

So to summarize: do you love the problem, do real users want it, is the timing right, and are you willing to be a beginner again. If I can say yes to all four, I take it seriously. If it's only the first one, it's probably a hobby, which is also perfectly fine.

r001.rationale: The response discusses timing generally, but does not say that consensus makes an opportunity too late unless the founder has far greater resources.

r002.rationale: It does not identify physical capacity as a limit on sustained founder effort.

r003.rationale: It asks whether the founder is willing to be a beginner and excited by the challenge, but does not say the opportunity must coincide with a period when the founder is willing to strive.

r004.rationale: The response does not mention family caregiving responsibilities or their effect on startup intensity.

r005.rationale: It recommends caring about the problem and looking for real users, but does not identify a large market as part of the choice.

astra-6.text:
For me, I’d start with three questions: Is this a problem I really care about? Do I have something distinctive to contribute? And is there evidence that people actually need what we could build?

A technically interesting problem is a good starting point, but it isn’t enough to make a company. I’d want to talk to potential users, build something small, and see whether it makes a meaningful difference for them. Then I’d ask myself whether I’m willing to spend years on it, including the parts that aren’t technically exciting. If those answers line up, that’s an opportunity worth pursuing.

r005.rationale: It combines personal interest with evidence of user need, but does not identify a large market.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, it starts with the problem. Is it something I care about enough to spend years working on? Then I ask whether I have a particular insight or technical advantage that could make a meaningful difference. A market can be attractive, but that alone doesn’t make it the right opportunity for me.

I also want to test the idea with real users. Can we build something small, put it in their hands, and see whether it solves a problem they actually have? Their response helps distinguish an interesting technical project from a business. And finally, I think about the people: do we share the same ambition, and can we work through uncertainty together?

r001.rationale: The candidate says market attractiveness alone is insufficient, but does not discuss consensus timing or competitors’ resources.

r002.rationale: It does not identify physical capacity as a limit on sustained founder effort.

r003.rationale: It mentions caring about the problem and working on it for years, but does not say the opportunity must coincide with a period of willingness to strive.

r004.rationale: It does not mention caregiving responsibilities or their effect on startup intensity.

r005.rationale: It discusses personal interest and an attractive market separately, but does not recommend choosing an opportunity at their intersection.
